nodes.name: Line
nodes.statement: A line $L := (x,y)$ is defined by two points $x,y\in\mathbb{C}$ with $x\ne y$ and a set $$l:=\{\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}.$$ We say two lines are equal if their generated set is equal.
nodes.section: 1.1 Defining lines, circles and the set of constructable points
nodes.label: def:line

nodes.statement: To express lines in the most general way, they are stated without the requirement that $x\ne y$, which allows for trivial lines. The condition is only included in the lemmas that require it.

nodes.name: Circle
nodes.statement: A circle $C := (c,r)$ is defined by a center $c$ with $c\in\mathbb{C}$, a radius $r\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and the set: $$c:=\{z\in\mathbb{C} \mid\|z-c\|=r\}.$$ We say two circles are equal if their underlying sets are equal.
nodes.section: 1.1 Defining lines, circles and the set of constructable points
nodes.label: def:circle

nodes.name: Set of lines
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{L(M)}$ is the set of all real straight lines $l$, with $| l\cap \mathcal{M} |\ge 2$. As a set this is: \begin{equation*} \mathcal{L(M)} := \{l \mid l = \{x,y\} \text{ with }x,y \in \mathcal{M} \land x \neq y\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1.1 Defining lines, circles and the set of constructable points
nodes.label: def:set_of_lines

nodes.name: Set of circles
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{C(M)}$ is the set of all circles in $\mathbb{C}$, with center in $\mathcal{M}$ and radius of $\mathcal{C}$ which is the distance of two points in $\mathcal{M}$. As an equation this is: $$\mathcal{C(M)}:=\{c\mid c = \langle c, \text{ dist } r_1 r_2 \rangle \text{ with } c,r_1,r_2\in M\}.$$
nodes.section: 1.1 Defining lines, circles and the set of constructable points
nodes.label: def:set_of_circles

nodes.name: Rules to construct a point
nodes.statement: We define operations that can be used to construct new points. \begin{enumerate} \item $(ILL)$ is the intersection of two different lines in $\mathcal{L(M)}$. \item $(ILC)$ is the intersection of a line in $\mathcal{L(M)}$ and a circle in $\mathcal{C(M)}$. \item $(ICC)$ is the intersection of two different circles in $\mathcal{C(M)}$. \end{enumerate} $ICL(\mathcal{M})$ is the union of all points that can be constructed using the operations $(ILL)$, $(ILC)$ and $(ICC)$ and $\mathcal{M}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Defining lines, circles and the set of constructable points
nodes.label: def:rules_to_constructed_a_point

nodes.name: Set of constructable points
nodes.statement: We inductively define the chain \begin{equation*} \mathcal{M}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{M}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{M}_2 \subseteq \dots \end{equation*} with $\mathcal{M}_0 = \mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{n+1} = ICL(\mathcal{M}_n)$\newline and call $\mathcal{M}_{\infty} = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \mathcal{M}_n$ the set of all constructable points.
nodes.section: 1.1 Defining lines, circles and the set of constructable points
nodes.label: def:set_of_constructable_points

nodes.statement: The set of points of a line $l$ is not defined by one position vector, i.e. for every $\alpha\in l$ $\{\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\} = \{\lambda x+\lambda y+\alpha\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}$.
nodes.label: lem:line_pionts_iff

nodes.statement: Two sets are equal if they have the same elements. Since $\alpha$ is in $l$, there exists a $\lambda_{\alpha}$ such that $\alpha = \lambda_{\alpha} x+(1-\lambda_{\alpha})y$. "$\Rightarrow:$" Let $z=\lambda_0 x + (1-\lambda_0)y$ (i.e. $z\in\{\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}$), we have to show that $z\in \{\lambda x+\lambda y+\alpha\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}$, which is equivalent to the existence of $\lambda$ such that $z = \lambda x+\lambda y+\alpha$. If we use $\lambda = \lambda_0 - \lambda_{\alpha} $ we get $$(\lambda_0 - \lambda_{\alpha}) x + ((\lambda_0 - \lambda_{\alpha}))y + \alpha \overset{\alpha = \lambda_{\alpha} x+(1-\lambda_{\alpha})y}{=} \lambda_0 x - \lambda_0 y + y = z$$ $\Leftarrow:$ Let $z$ be in $\{\lambda x+(\lambda)y+\alpha\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}$, if we use $\lambda = \lambda_0 + \lambda_{\alpha} $ we get $$(\lambda_0 + \lambda_{\alpha}) x + (1 -(\lambda_0 + \lambda_{\alpha}))y = \lambda_0 x - \lambda_0 y + \lambda_{\alpha} x - \lambda_{\alpha} y + y \overset{\alpha = \lambda_{\alpha} x+(1-\lambda_{\alpha})y}{=} \lambda_0 (x - y) + \alpha = z$$

nodes.name: parallel
nodes.statement: Two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are parallel if they have the same slope, i.e. $\exists r\in\mathbb{C}: l_1 = \{x + r \mid x\in l_2\}$.
nodes.label: def:parallel

nodes.name: Parallel defined by basis
nodes.statement: If the basis of two lines is moved by the same amount, i.e $l_1.z_1 - l_2.z_1 = l_1.z_2- l_2.z_2$, then they are parallel.
nodes.label: lem:parallel_by_basis

nodes.statement: We have to lines $l_1, l_2$ with basis $z_1, z_2$ and $l_1.z_1 - l_2.z_1 = l_1.z_2- l_2.z_2$. To show that they are parallel we have to show that $$\exists r: l_1 = \{z + r \mid z\in l_2\}.$$ To make it easier to read we define $a := l_1.z_1$, $b:= l_1.z_2$, $x:= l_2.z_1$ and $y:= l_2.z_2$.\\ Upon unravelling the definition, it becomes evident that we need to show that $\exists t: t \cdot a +(1-t)\cdot b=z \iff \exists s :s \cdot x+(1-s)y+(a-x)=z$.\\ $\Rightarrow:$ Claim $s = \frac{t(a-b)}{x-y}$ is a solution.\\ "$\Leftarrow:$" Claim $t = \frac{s(x-y)}{a-b}$ is a solution.

\begin{align*} && z &= s \cdot x+(1-s)y+(a-x)&&| z= t\cdot a+(1-t)\cdot b\\ &\Leftrightarrow & t\cdot a+(1-t)\cdot b &= s \cdot x+(1-s)y+(a-x)\\ &\Leftrightarrow & t\cdot a-t\cdot b +b &= s \cdot x-s\cdot y + y+(a-x)&& | -y\\ &\Leftrightarrow & t\cdot a-t\cdot b + b-y &= s \cdot x-s\cdot y+(a-x)-y&&| a-x =b-y\\ &\Leftrightarrow & t\cdot a-t\cdot b &= s \cdot x+s\cdot y\\ &\Leftrightarrow & t(a-b) &= s(x-y)&&|s:= \frac{t(a-b)}{x-y}\\ &\Leftrightarrow & t(a-b) &= \frac{t(a-b)}{x-y}(x-y)\\ &\Leftrightarrow & t(a-b) &= t(a-b) \end{align*}

\begin{align*} && t\cdot a+(1-t)b &= z&&| z:= s \cdot x+(1-s)y+(a-x)\\ &\Leftrightarrow& t\cdot a-t\cdot b+b &= s \cdot x-s\cdot y+y+(a-x)&&|-y;a-x =b-y\\ &\Leftrightarrow& t(a-b) &= s(x-y)&&|t:= \frac{s(x-y)}{a-b}\\ &\Leftrightarrow& \frac{s(x-y)}{a-b}(a-b) &= s(x-y) \end{align*}
The direction vector of a line $l$ is the vector $l.z_1 - l.z_2$.
nodes.label: def:direction_vector

nodes.statement: Two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are \emph{parallel'} if there exists a $k$ such that $l_1.z_1 - l_1.z_2 = k \cdot (l_2.z_1 - l_2.z_2)$.
nodes.label: def:parallel'

nodes.name: Parallel imp parallel'
nodes.statement: If two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are parallel' they are parallel.
nodes.label: lem:parallel_iff_parallel'

nodes.statement: The other direction holds as well, but is not needed.

Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be two lines with $l_1.z_1 - l_1.z_2 = k \cdot (l_2.z_1 - l_2.z_2)$. We have to show that $l_1 = \{z + r \mid z\in l_2\}$, i.e. $\exists r: l_1 = \{z + r \mid z\in l_2\}$.\\ First we remark that $k\ne 0$ since $l_1.z_1\ne l_1.z_2$. We define $r:= y_1 - y_2$ and show that $l_1 = \{z + r \mid z\in l_2\}$. For $z$ to be in $l_1$ is equivalent to $z = \lambda x_1 + (1-\lambda)y_1$ for some $\lambda_0$. For $z$ to be in $\{x + y_1-y_2 \mid z\in l_2\}$ is wquivalent to the existence of $\lambda$ such that $$z = \lambda x_2 + (1-\lambda)y_2 + y_1 - y_2 = \lambda (x_2 - y_2) + y_1 \overset{\lambda = \lambda_0 * k}{=} \lambda_0 k (x_2-x_2)-y_1\overset{x_1-y_1=k(x_2-y_2)}{=}\lambda_0(x_1-y_1)+y_1.$$

nodes.name: Parallel imp equal
nodes.statement: If two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are parallel' and intersect, then they are equal.
nodes.label: lem:eq_of_parallel

nodes.statement: Let $z\in l_1 \cap l_2$. Then we use lemma \ref{lem:line_pionts_iff} to get $l_1 = l_2 \Leftrightarrow \{\lambda (x_1-y_1)\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\} = \{\lambda (x_2- y_2)+z\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}$. Since for every $\lambda$ we have $\lambda (x_1-y_2) + x = \lambda \cdot k(x_2- y_2)+z$ we get $l_1 = l_2$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{M}\subseteq ICL(\mathcal{M})$
nodes.statement: Every set $M$ is included in the constructable points of $M$, i.e. \[M \subseteq ICL(M)\]
nodes.label: lem:M_in_ICL_M

nodes.statement: Follows from the definition of $ICL(M)$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{M}_i$ Monoton
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{M}_i$ is monoton, i.e. $$\mathcal{M}_i \subseteq \mathcal{M}_{i+1}.$$ This can be generalised to $$\forall m :\forall n\le m : \mathcal{M}_n \subseteq \mathcal{M}_m.$$
nodes.label: lem:M_i_monoton

nodes.statement: Follows from the definition of $\mathcal{M}_i$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathcal{M}_i$
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{M}$ is in $\mathcal{M}_i$, i.e. $$\mathcal{M} \subseteq \mathcal{M}_i.$$
nodes.label: lem:M_in_Mi

nodes.statement: Combining the fact that $\mathcal{M}_0 = \mathcal{M}$ \ref{def:set_of_constructable_points} and the monotonity of $\mathcal{M}_i$ \ref{lem:M_i_monoton} we get the result.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{M}_i$ in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{M}_i$ is in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$, i.e. $$\mathcal{M}_i \subseteq \mathcal{M}_{\infty}.$$
nodes.label: lem:M_i_in_M_inf

nodes.statement: Follows from the definition of $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{M}$ is in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:M_in_M_inf

nodes.statement: Combining $\mathcal{M} \subseteq \mathcal{M}_i$ \ref{lem:M_in_Mi} and $\mathcal{M}_i \subseteq \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ \ref{lem:M_i_in_M_inf} we get the result.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ iff $\mathcal{M}_i$
nodes.statement: A point $z$ is in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ if and only if $z$ is in $\mathcal{M}_i$ for some $i$.
nodes.label: lem:M_inf_iff_M_i

nodes.statement: Follows from the definition of $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: $L(\mathcal{M_{\infty}})$ iff $L(\mathcal{M_i})$
nodes.statement: A line $l$ is in $\mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ if and only if $l$ is in $\mathcal{L(M_i)}$ for some $i$.
nodes.label: cor:L_M_inf_iff_L_M_i

nodes.statement: Follows from \ref{lem:M_inf_iff_M_i} and the fact that every line in $\mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ is defined by two points in $\mathcal{M_{\infty}}$.

nodes.name: $C(\mathcal{M_{\infty}})$ iff $C(\mathcal{M_i})$
nodes.statement: A circle $c$ is in $\mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$ if and only if $c$ is in $\mathcal{C(M_i)}$ for some $i$.
nodes.label: cor:C_M_inf_iff_C_M_i

nodes.statement: Follows from \ref{lem:M_inf_iff_M_i} and the fact that every circle in $\mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$ is defined by three points in $\mathcal{M_{\infty}}$.

nodes.name: Intersection of lines in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: For two lines $l_1, l_2 \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ is $l_1 \cap l_2 \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:ill_M_inf

nodes.statement: By corollary \ref{cor:L_M_inf_iff_L_M_i} and the monotonity of $\mathcal{M}_i$ \ref{lem:M_i_monoton} we get that there exists an $n$ such that $l_1, l_2 \in \mathcal{L(M_n)}$. Therfore $l_1 \cap l_2 \in \mathcal{M}_{n+1} \stackrel{\ref{lem:M_i_in_M_inf}}{\subseteq} \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.
To formalise the lemmas \ref{lem:M_inf_iff_M_i}, \ref{cor:L_M_inf_iff_L_M_i} and \ref{cor:C_M_inf_iff_C_M_i} one should use filters in Lean.

nodes.name: Intersection of line and circle in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: For a line $l \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ and a circle $c \in \mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$ is $l \cap c \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:ilc_M_inf

nodes.statement: By corollary \ref{cor:L_M_inf_iff_L_M_i} and \ref{cor:C_M_inf_iff_C_M_i} we get that there exists an $n$ such that $l \in \mathcal{L(M_n)}$ and $c \in \mathcal{C(M_n)}$. Therfore $l \cap c \in \mathcal{M}_{n+1} \stackrel{\text{\ref{lem:M_i_in_M_inf}}}{\subseteq} \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Intersection of circles in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: For two circles $c_1, c_2 \in \mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$ it follows that $c_1 \cap c_2 \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:icc_M_inf

nodes.statement: By corollary \ref{cor:C_M_inf_iff_C_M_i} we get that there exists an $n$ such that $c_1, c_2 \in \mathcal{C(M_n)}$. Therfore $c_1 \cap c_2 \in \mathcal{M}_{n+1} \stackrel{\ref{lem:M_i_in_M_inf}}{\subseteq} \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Negative complex numbers
nodes.statement: For $z \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $-z \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_neg

nodes.statement: Define $l = \{0,z\}$ and $c = \{0,\text{ dist } (0, z)\}$.\\ By assumption $0, z \in M_{\infty}$, so $l \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ and $c \in \mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$.\\ \underline{Claim 1}: $-z$ is in $l$. \underline{Claim 2}: $-z$ is in $c$. By claim 1 and 2 we get that $-z \in l \cap c$. Futhermore $-z $ is in $M_{\infty}$, after lemma \ref{lem:ilc_M_inf}.
By the definition of $l:=\{\lambda 0+(1-\lambda)z\mid\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}$ with $\lambda = 2$ we get $2 \cdot 0 + (1-2)z = -z$.
Unfolding the definition of $c:=\{x\in\mathbb{C} \mid\|x-0\|=\text{ dist } (0\ z)\}$. By the definition of the distance we get $\|0-(-z)\| = \text{ dist } (0\ z)$.

nodes.name: Addition of complex numbers
nodes.statement: For $z_1, z_2 \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $z_1 + z_2 \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_add

Using that $c_2$ ia definded as $c_2:=\{x\in\mathbb{C} \mid\|x-z_2\|=\text{ dist } (0\ z_1)\}$ and the definition of the distance we get $\|z_2-(z_1+z_2)\| = \text{ dist } (0\ z_1)$.

nodes.name: Subtraction of complex numbers
nodes.statement: For $z_1, z_2 \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $z_1 - z_2 \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: cor:construction_sub

nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:construction_neg} and \ref{lem:construction_add} we get $z_1 - z_2 = z_1 + (-z_2) \in M_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Construction of parallel lines
nodes.statement: For $l \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ and $z \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $\exists l' \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ with $z\in l'$ and $l\|l'$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_parallel_lines

nodes.statement: Let $l$ be a line through $x,y \in \mathcal{M_{\infty}}$ and $z \in \mathcal{M_{\infty}}$.\\ After corollary \ref{cor:construction_sub} we get $z - x \in \mathcal{M_{\infty}}$ and therfore $z-x + y \in \mathcal{M_{\infty}}$\ref{lem:construction_add}.\\ Define $l' = \{z, z-x+y\}$, then $l' \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ and since a line is defined by two points and we moved them the same distance ($z-x$) $l'$ is parallel to $l$.\ref{lem:parallel_by_basis}

nodes.name: Complex conjugation
nodes.statement: For $z \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $\overline{z} \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_conj

nodes.statement: Define $c_1 = \{0,\text{ dist } (0, z)\}$ and $c_2 = \{1,\text{ dist } (1, z)\}$.\\ By assumption $0, 1, z \in M_{\infty}$, so $c_1, c_2 \in \mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$.\\ \underline{Claim 1}: $\overline{z}$ is in $c_1$. \underline{Claim 2}: $\overline{z}$ is in $c_2$. By claim 1 and 2 we get that $\overline{z} \in c_1 \cap c_2$. Futhermore $\overline{z} $ is in $M_{\infty}$, after lemma \ref{lem:icc_M_inf}.

The definition of $c_1$ can be written in the following form: $$\{x\in\mathbb{C} \mid \|x-0\| = \text{ dist } (0\ z)\}.$$ Using the definition of the distance, we obtain the following result: $$\|0 - \overline{z}\| = \|\overline{z}\| = \|z\| = \text{ dist } (0\ z).$$

From the definition of $c_2:=\{x\in\mathbb{C} \mid\|x-1\|=\text{ dist } (1\ z)\}$ and the definition of the distance, we can derive the following: $$\|1-\overline{z}\| = \|\overline{z}-1\| = \sqrt{(\Re(\overline{z})-1)^2 + \Im(\overline{z})^2} = \sqrt{(\Re(z)-1)^2 + \Im(z)^2} = \|z-1\|=\text{ dist } (1\ z).$$

nodes.name: Construction $\imath r\in\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: For $r \in \mathbb{R}\cap M_{\infty}$ it follows that $\imath\cdot r \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_imath_r

nodes.statement: First we construct the imaginary axis. Define $c_1 = \{-1,2\}$ and $c_2 = \{1,2\}$.\\ \underline{Claim 1}: $c_1, c_2 \in \mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$ \underline{Claim 2}: $\imath\sqrt{3}$ and $-\imath\sqrt{3}$ are in $c_1 \cap c_2$. Now we define $l = \{\imath\sqrt{3}, -\imath\sqrt{3}\}$.\\ \underline{Claim 3}: $l \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ To get $\imath r$ we define $c = \{0,|r|\}$.\\ \underline{Claim 4}: $\imath r$ is in $c \cap l$. Therfore $\imath r \in M_{\infty}$ after lemma \ref{lem:ilc_M_inf}.
By assumption and lemma \ref{lem:construction_neg} we get $-1, 1 \in M_{\infty}$. Using $\text{ dist }(-1 1)=2$ we get $c_1, c_2 \in \mathcal{C(M_{\infty})}$, by the definition of the circle.

Unfolding the definition of $c_1:=\{x\in\mathbb{C} \mid\|x+1\|=2\}$ and $c_2:=\{x\in\mathbb{C} \mid\|x-1\|=2\}$. By the definition of the distance we get $\|-\imath\sqrt{3}+1\| = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2$ and $\|\imath\sqrt{3}-1\| = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2$.
By claim 2 and \ref{lem:icc_M_inf} we get $\imath\sqrt{3}, -\imath\sqrt{3} \in M_{\infty}$, so $l \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$.

It is clear that $\imath r \in c$. Now using the definition of $l$ and $\lambda = \frac{r}{2\sqrt{3}+\frac{1}{2}}$ we get $(\frac{r}{2\sqrt{3}+\frac{r}{2}})\imath\sqrt{3} + (1-\frac{r}{2\sqrt{3}+\frac{r}{2}})(-\imath\sqrt{3}) = \imath r$.

nodes.name: Construction of $\imath$
nodes.statement: $\imath \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: cor:construction_imath

nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:construction_imath_r} with $r = 1$ and the definition of $\mathcal{M}$ we get $\imath \in M_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Construction of real part
nodes.statement: For $z \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $z.re \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_real

nodes.statement: Without loss of generality we can assume that $z \in \mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$.\\ Define the lines $l = \{z, \overline{z}\}$ and $l_{\Re} = \{1, 0\}$.\\ By using Lemma \ref{lem:construction_conj}, they are in $\mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$.\\ To show that $z.re \in l \cap l_{\Re}$ we use $t:= 1/2$ for $l$ and $t:= z.re$ for $l_{\Re}$.

nodes.name: Construction of imaginary part
nodes.statement: For $z \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $z.im \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_imag

nodes.statement: Define the lines $l = \{z, z-1\}$ and $l_{\Im} = \{\imath, 0\}$.\\ Now it is analog to the proof of lemma \ref{lem:construction_real}, that $z.im \cdot \imath \in l \cap l_{\Im}$. Now we can project $z.im \cdot \imath + 0$ on the real axis by drawing a circle with center $0$ and radius $\|z.im\|$ and taking the intersection with the real axis.

nodes.name: $z \in M_{\infty} \Rightarrow z.re, z.im \in M_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: For $z \in \mathbb{C}$. $z$ is in $M_{\infty}$ if and only if $z.re, z.im \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: cor:z_iff_re_im_M_inf

nodes.statement: "$\Rightarrow$:" If $z \in M_{\infty}$ then $z.re, z.im \in M_{\infty}$ after lemma \ref{lem:construction_real} and \ref{lem:construction_imag}.\\ "$\Leftarrow$:" If $z.re, z.im \in M_{\infty}$ then $z.re + \imath z.im \in M_{\infty}$ after lemma \ref{lem:construction_add} and lemma \ref{lem:construction_imath_r}.

nodes.name: Multiplication of positve real numbers
nodes.statement: For $a, b \in M_{\infty}\cap\mathbb{R}$ it follows that $a \cdot b \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_mul

nodes.statement: Define the three lines $l = \{a+\imath b - \imath, \imath b\}$ and $l_{\Re} = \{1,0\}$.\\ \underline{Claim 1}: $l \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ \underline{Claim 2}: $l_{\Re} \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ To show that $a\cdot b \in M_{\infty}$ we need to show that $l \cap l_{\Re} \in M_{\infty}$\ref{lem:ill_M_inf}. That $ab \in l_{\Re} \cap l$ is clear after definition $t=ab$. For $ab \in l$ we use $t=b$ and get $t(a+\imath b - \imath) + (1-t)\imath b \stackrel{t:=b}{=}ba + \imath b^2 -\imath b + \imath b -\imath b^2 = a\cdot b$.

By assumption $b \in M_{\infty}$ so after Lemma \ref{lem:construction_imath_r} $\imath b \in M_{\infty}$. Futhermore $l_2 \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ after Claim 1 and Lemma \ref{lem:construction_parallel_lines}.
By assumption $0, 1 \in M_{\infty}$, so $l_{\Re} \in \mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$.
This construction uses parallel lines, but it is not needed for the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Multiplication of complex numbers
nodes.statement: For $z_1, z_2 \in M_{\infty}$ it follows that $z_1 \cdot z_2$ in $M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: cor:construction_mul_complex

nodes.statement: Let $z_1 = a + \imath b$ and $z_2 = c + \imath d$. Then $$z_1 \cdot z_2 = (a + \imath b) \cdot (c + \imath d) = (a \cdot c - b \cdot d) + \imath (a \cdot d + b \cdot c).$$ By combining the Lemmas \ref{lem:construction_mul}, \ref{lem:construction_add}, \ref{cor:construction_sub}, \ref{lem:construction_real} and \ref{lem:construction_imag} we get that $z_1 \cdot z_2 \in M_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Invers of a pos real number
nodes.statement: If $a \in M_{\infty}\cap\mathbb{R}$, then $a^{-1}$ is in $M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_inv

nodes.statement: The proof is analogous to that of Lemma \ref{lem:construction_mul}. It requires only two lines: $l = \{1 - \imath z + \imath, \imath\}$ and $l_{\Re} = \{1,0\}$.\\ With out loss of generality we can assume that $a \ne 0$.\\ The fact that they are in $\mathcal{L(M_{\infty})}$ follows analog to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:construction_mul}.\\ Thus we have just to show that $z^{-1} \in l$, i.e. $\exists t: t (1 - \imath a + \imath) + (1 - t) I = a^{-1}$ $$t (1 - \imath a + \imath) + (1 - t) \imath \stackrel{t:=a^{-1}}{=} a^{-1} - a^{-1} \imath a + a^{-1}\imath + \imath - a^{-1}\imath = a^{-1}.$$ The rest follows analog.

nodes.name: Inverse of a complex number
nodes.statement: If $z \in M_{\infty}$, then $z^{-1}$ is in $M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: cor:inv_M_inf

nodes.statement: For $z \in M_{\infty}$ we can write $z = a + \imath b$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $$z^{-1} = \frac{1}{z} = \frac{\overline{z}}{z\overline{z}} = \frac{a - \imath b}{a^2+b^2}= (a - \imath b) \cdot (aa+bb)^{-1}.$$ It is now possible to combine the lemmas for addition \ref{lem:construction_add}, subtraction \ref{cor:construction_sub}, multiplication \ref{cor:construction_mul_complex} and the corollary for the inverse of a positive real number \ref{lem:construction_inv} with the part concerning the existence of real and imaginary components \ref{cor:z_iff_re_im_M_inf} in order to conclude that $z^{-1} \in M_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Angle in $M_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: If $0 \ne z = r\cdot e^{\imath\alpha} \in M_{\infty}$, then $e^{\imath\alpha} \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:angle_M_inf

nodes.statement: Let $l$ be a line through $0$ and $z$ and $c$ be the unit circle. Then $l \cap c = \{e^{\imath\alpha}\}$. The rest follows from the construction of the intersection of a line and a circle\ref{lem:icc_M_inf}.

nodes.name: Midpoint in $M_{\infty}$
nodes.statement: If $z_1, z_2 \in M_{\infty}$, then $\frac{z_1 + z_2}{2} \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: cor:Construction.midpoiont

nodes.statement: Combining the lemmas for addition\ref{lem:construction_add}, multiplication\ref{cor:construction_mul_complex} and the invers of a complex number\ref{cor:inv_M_inf} we get that $\frac{z_1 + z_2}{1+1} \in M_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Halving of an angle
nodes.statement: For $\alpha \in [0,2\pi)$, if $e^{\imath\alpha} \in M_{\infty}$, then $e^{\imath\frac{\alpha}{2}} \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:Construction.angle_half_M_inf

nodes.statement: For $\alpha \ne 0 \ne \pi$ we take the intersection of the unit circle with the line through $0$ and and the mipiont of $e^{\imath\alpha}$ and $1$. For $\alpha = 0$ we get $e^{\imath\frac{\alpha}{2}} = 1$ and for $\alpha = \pi$ we get $e^{\imath\frac{\alpha}{2}} =\imath + 0$.

nodes.name: Construction of radius
nodes.statement: If $z = r\cdot e^{\imath\alpha} \in M_{\infty}$, then $r \in M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:construction_radius

nodes.statement: The radius is the distance from $0$ to $z$, which is the same as $\|z\|$.
We use the fact that $r = \|z\| = \sqrt{\Re(z)^2 + \Im(z)^2}$. Since we have spilt $r$ in already constructed parts, we get that $r \in M_{\infty}$.

nodes.name: Root of pos real number
nodes.statement: If $r \in M_{\infty}\cap\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, then $\sqrt{r}$ is in $M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: lem:pos_real_root

nodes.statement: Without loss of generality we can assume that $r \ge 1$. Otherwise we can use the fact that $\sqrt{r} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{r^{-1}}}$. The initial step is to define the following lines and circles: \begin{itemize} \item [$l_1$] $:= \{z_1 :=1; z_2 := \imath + 1\}$ \item [$l_{\Re}$] $:= \{z_1:=0; z_2:= 1\}$ \item [$c_1$] $:= \{\text{center}:= \frac{r}{2}; \text{radius} := \text{ dist } (0,\frac{r}{2})\}$ \item [$c_2$] $:= \{\text{center}:= 0; \text{radius} := \text{ dist } (0,\sqrt{r})\}$ \end{itemize} It can be observed that both $l_1$ and $l_{\Re}$ are elements of $L(M)$, and that $c_1$ is an element of $C(M)$. Furthermore, it can be demonstrated that the $\sqrt{r}$ is an element of $l_{\Re} \cap c_2$. Consequently, the only remaining step is to show that $c_2$ is an element of $C(M)$, which is equivalent to proving that there exists a $z$ in $M_{\infty}$ that is also an element of $c_2$. This is possible since $0$ is an element of $M_{\infty}$.\\ \underline{Claim}: There exists a $z \in l_1 \cap c_1$, such that $z \in c_2$. Therefore, it can be concluded that $\sqrt{r}$ is also constructible.

In accordance with the theorem of Pythagoras, it can be demonstrated that$z= 1 \pm \imath \sqrt{r-1}$. A further application of the Pythagorean theorem yields the following result: $$\text{ dist } (0,z) \overset{z= 1 + \imath \sqrt{r-1}}{=} \sqrt{1^2 + (\sqrt{r-1})^2} = \sqrt{1 + r - 1} = \sqrt{r} = \text{ dist } (0,\sqrt{r}).$$

nodes.name: Square root of a complexnumber
nodes.statement: If $z \in M_{\infty}$, then $\sqrt{z}$ is in $M_{\infty}$.
nodes.label: cor:root_M_inf

nodes.statement: $z = r \cdot e^{\imath \alpha}$ with $r \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\sqrt{z} = \sqrt{r} \cdot e^{\imath \frac{\alpha}{2}}$. Now we can use Lemma \ref{lem:construction_radius} and Lemma \ref{lem:pos_real_root} to get that $\sqrt{z} \in M_{\infty}$. For $e^{\imath \frac{\alpha}{2}}$ we can combine Lemma \ref{lem:angle_M_inf} and Lemma \ref{lem:Construction.angle_half_M_inf}. Now we get that $\sqrt{z} \in M_{\infty}$, after Lemma \ref{lem:construction_mul}.
For $M\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ with $0,1 \in M$. $M_{\infty}$ is a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.label: thm:MField

nodes.statement: To show that $M_{\infty}$ is a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ we have to show that $0,1\in M_{\infty}$ and $M_{\infty}$ is closed under addition, multiplication, subtraction and division. \begin{itemize} \item [$0,1$:] This follows from $0,1 \in M$ and Lemma \ref{lem:M_in_M_inf}. \item [$+$:] For $z_1,z_2 \in M_{\infty}$ we can construct $z_1 + z_2 \in M_{\infty}$. \ref{lem:construction_add} \item [$*$:] For $z_1,z_2 \in M_{\infty}$ we can construct $z_1 \cdot z_2 \in M_{\infty}$. \ref{cor:construction_mul_complex} \item [$-$:] For $z \in M_{\infty}$ we can construct $-z \in M_{\infty}$. \ref{lem:construction_neg} \item [$^{-1}$:] For $z \in M_{\infty}$ with $z \ne 0$ we can construct $z^{-1} \in M_{\infty}$. \ref{cor:inv_M_inf} \end{itemize}
To prove that $M_{\infty}$ is a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ in Lean we have to create a new instance with carrier $M_{\infty}$.
Since $M_{\infty}$ is a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$, $M_{\infty}$ is a field which is automatically proved in Lean, by \lstinline{infer_instance}.
nodes.label: rem:MField_Field

nodes.statement: For $M\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ with $0,1 \in M$ it holds: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\imath \in M_{\infty}$. \item[(ii)] For $z = x + \imath y \in \mathbb{C}$ the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $z \in M_{\infty}$. \item $x, y \in M_{\infty}$. \item $x, \imath y \in M_{\infty}$. \end{enumerate} \item[(iii)] For $0 \ne z = r \exp(\imath \alpha) \in \mathbb{C}$ the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $z \in M_{\infty}$. \item $r,\exp(\imath \alpha) \in M_{\infty}$. \end{enumerate} \end{itemize}
nodes.label: lem:M_inf_properties

nodes.statement: This lemma is a direct consequence of section \ref{basic_constructions}. \begin{itemize} \item[(i):] We can apply construction \ref{cor:construction_imath} \item[(ii):] We can apply construction \ref{cor:z_iff_re_im_M_inf} and \ref{cor:construction_imath}. \item[(iii):] We can apply construction \ref{lem:construction_radius} and \ref{lem:angle_M_inf}. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: quadratic closed field
nodes.statement: A field $F$ is called \emph{quadratic closed} if for all $x \in F$ there is a $y \in F$ such that $y^2 = x$.
nodes.label: def:quadritc_closed_field

nodes.statement: An equivalent definition is that $F$ is quadratic closed if $F=\{a^2\mid a \in F\}$.
For $M\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ with $0,1 \in M$, $M_{\infty}$ is quadratic closed.
nodes.label: lem:M_inf_quad_closed

nodes.statement: It is established that $M_{\infty}$ is a field (see remark \ref{rem:MField_Field}). Furthermore, the corollary \ref{cor:root_M_inf} provides a root $z^{\frac{1}{2}}$ of $z \in M_{\infty}$. $$ z^{\frac{1}{2}} * z^{\frac{1}{2}} = z^{\frac{1}{2}^2} = z^{2\cdot \frac{1}{2}} = z.$$ Therefore $M_{\infty}$ is quadratic closed.
For a Set $M \subset \mathbb{C}$ we define the \emph{conjugate set} of $M$ as \begin{equation*} Conj(M) = \{\overline{z}\mid z\in M\} \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:conj_set

nodes.statement: For two sets $M,N \subset \mathbb{C}$ $$Conj(M\cup N) = Conj(M) \cup Conj(N).$$
nodes.label: lem:conj_union

nodes.statement: For $z \in Conj(M\cup N)$ there is a $w \in M\cup N$ such that $\overline{w} = z$, therefore $ z = \overline{w} \in Conj(M) \cup Conj(N)$. The other direction is analog.
For a set $M \subset \mathbb{C}$ it holds that $Conj(Conj(M)) = M$.
nodes.label: lem:conj_conj_id

nodes.statement: $$Conj(Conj(M)) = Conj(\{\overline{z}\mid z\in M\}) = \{\overline{\overline{z}}\mid z\in M\} = \{ z \mid z\in M\} = M.$$
We call a subset of $\mathbb{C}$ \emph{conjugate closed} if $M= Conj(M)$.
nodes.label: def:conj_closed

nodes.statement: $M_{\infty}$ is conjugate closed.
nodes.label: lem:conj_MField

nodes.statement: We can apply construction \ref{lem:construction_conj} and the fact that $\overline{\overline z} = z$ for all $z \in\mathbb{C}$.
For $M\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ $M\cup Conj(M)$ is conjugate closed.
nodes.label: lem:M_con_M

nodes.statement: We can apply Lemma \ref{lem:conj_union} and \ref{lem:conj_conj_id}. $$Conj(M\cup Conj(M)) = Conj(M) \cup Conj(Conj(M)) = M \cup Conj(M).$$
The set of rational numbers is conjugate closed.
nodes.label: lem:ConjClosed.Rat_ConjClosed

nodes.statement: For every $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ we have $\overline{r} = r$.
For $M,N \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ with $M \subseteq N$ it holds that $Conj(M) \subseteq Conj(N)$.
nodes.label: lem:ConjClosed.conj_inclusion

nodes.statement: For $z \in Conj(M)$ there is a $w \in M$ such that $\overline{w} = z$ and since $M \subseteq N$ we have $w \in N$ and therefore $z \in Conj(N)$.
For a subfield $F$ of $\mathbb{C}$ the conjugate set $Conj(F)$ is a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.label: lem:ConjClosed.conj_field

nodes.statement: We have to show that $0,1 \in Conj(F)$ and $Conj(F)$ is closed under addition, multiplication, negation and inversion. \begin{itemize} \item [$0,1$:] Since $0,1 \in F$ and $\overline{0} = 0, \overline{1} = 1$ we have $0,1 \in Conj(F)$. \item [$+$:] For $z_1,z_2 \in F$ we have $\overline{z_1 + z_2} = \Re(z_1 + z_2) - \imath\cdot \Im(z_1 + z_2) = \Re(z_1) + \Re(z_2) - \imath\cdot (\Im(z_1) + \Im(z_2)) = \overline{z_1} + \overline{z_2}$. Therefore $Conj(F)$ is closed under addition. \item [$-$:] For $z \in F$ we have $\overline{-z} = \Re(-z) - \imath\cdot \Im(-z) = -(\Re(z) - \imath\cdot (\Im(z))) = -\overline{z}$. Therefore $Conj(F)$ is closed under negation. \item [$*$:] Since $\overline{z_1 \cdot z_2} = \overline{z_1} \cdot \overline{z_2}$ we have $Conj(F)$ is closed under multiplication. \item [$^{-1}$:] Since $\overline{z^{-1}} = \overline{z}^{-1}$ we have $Conj(F)$ is closed under inversion. \end{itemize}
Let $L$ be a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$, with $L = conj(L)$. For all $z = x + \imath y \in L$ we have $x, \imath y \in L$.
nodes.label: lem:ConjClosed.re_im_in_L

nodes.statement: Let $z = x + \imath y \in L$. Since $L$ is conjugate closed we know that $\overline{z}=x-\imath y \in L$. This implies \begin{equation*} \frac{z + \overline{z}}{2} = x \in L \end{equation*} and therefore also $\imath y = z - x \in L$.
Let $L$ be a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$, with $L = conj(L)$, and $z_1, z_2 \in L$. For $r := \|z_1-z_2\|$ we get that $r^2 \in L$.
nodes.label: lem:ConjClosed.distSq_L

nodes.statement: For $z_1 = x_1 + \imath y_1$ and $z_2 = x_2 + \imath y_2$ we have \begin{equation*} r = \|z_1 - z_2\| = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2} \end{equation*} and therefore \begin{equation*} r^2 = (x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2 \end{equation*} After applying Lemma \ref{lem:ConjClosed.re_im_in_L} we get $r^2 \in L$.

Initially, it is demonstrated that $z$ belongs to the intersection of $G_1$ and $G_2$, if and only if there exist real numbers $\lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$, such that the equations $1$, $2$ and $3$ are satisfied. Subsequently, it follows that $z$ is an element of $L$.\\ Equations $1$ and $2$ are equivalent to the following: $$ \lambda x_1 + (1 - \lambda)x_2 = \mu x_3 + (1 - \mu)x_4 $$ $$ \lambda y_1 + (1 - \lambda)y_2 = \mu y_3 + (1 - \mu)y_4 $$ This is the definition of $z \in G_1 \cap G_2$, expressed in terms of its real and imaginary parts.\\ The third equation is equivalent to $z = \lambda z_1 + (1 - \lambda)z_2$. This allows us to conclude that $z$ belongs to $G_1$ at the point where $G_1$ and $G_2$ intersect. Consequently, we can assume that $z$ belongs to the intersection of $G_1$ and $G_2$. Now we can show that $z$ is an element of $L$.\\ Since we know that z is equal to $\lambda z_1 + (1-\lambda)z_2$ and $z_1, z_2 \in L$ we only have to show that $\lambda \in L$. Here for we use the equations from the first part of the proof. \begin{align*} 1 &&\lambda(x_1 - x_2)+\mu(x_4-x_3) &= x_4-x_2\\ 2 &&\lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)+\mu(\imath y_4-\imath y_3) &= \imath y_4-\imath y_2 \end{align*} Now we solve 2 for $\mu$ \begin{align*} && \lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)+\mu(\imath y_4-\imath y_3) &= \imath y_4-\imath y_2 && \mid -\lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)\\ &\Leftrightarrow & \mu(\imath y_4-\imath y_3) &= \imath y_4-\imath y_2 - \lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2) && \mid \div \imath(y_4-y_3)\\ &\Leftrightarrow & \mu &= \frac{\imath y_4-\imath y_2 - \lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)}{\imath y_4-\imath y_3}\\ \end{align*} Since we divided by $\imath (y_4-y_3)$ we need to assume that $y_4 \ne y_3$, so we need to first handle the case $y_4 = y_3$.\\ If $y_4 = y_3$ we have $\lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2) = \imath y_4-\imath y_2$ and since $y_4 = y_3$ $y_1 \ne y_2$, because otherwise both Lines would be parallel to the real line and therefore $G_1 = G_2$ or $G_1 \cap G_2 = \varnothing$. Therefore $\lambda = \frac{\imath y_4-\imath y_2}{\imath y_1 - \imath y_2}$. Using the fact that real part and the imaginary part times $\imath + 0$ are in $L$ \ref{lem:ConjClosed.re_im_in_L} we have written $\lambda$ as a fraction of two elements in $L$. It can thus be concluded that $\lambda$ is in $L$, which implies that $z = \lambda z_1 + (1-\lambda)z_2$ is in $L$.\\ Now we insert $\mu$ in 1 and solve for $\lambda$.\\ \resizebox{1\linewidth}{!}{ \begin{minipage}{\linewidth} \begin{alignat*}{3} && \lambda(x_1 - x_2)+\mu(x_4-x_3) &= x_4-x_2 && \mid 1 \leftarrow 2\\ &\Leftrightarrow & \lambda(x_1 - x_2)+\frac{\imath y_4-\imath y_2 - \lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)}{\imath y_4-\imath y_3}(x_4-x_3) &= x_4-x_2 && \mid \cdot (\imath y_4-\imath y_3)\\ &\Leftrightarrow & \lambda(x_1 - x_2)(\imath y_4-\imath y_3)+(\imath y_4-\imath y_2 - \lambda(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2))(x_4-x_3) &= (x_4-x_2)(\imath y_4-\imath y_3) && \mid - (x_1 - x_2)(\imath y_4-\imath y_3)\\ &\Leftrightarrow & \lambda((x_1 - x_2)(\imath y_4-\imath y_3) - (\imath y_4-\imath y_2)(x_4-x_3)) &= (x_4-x_2)(\imath y_4-\imath y_3) - (\imath y_4-\imath y_2)(x_4-x_3) && \mid \div ((\imath y_4-\imath y_3)(x_1 - x_2)- (\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)(x_4-x_3))\\ &\Leftrightarrow & \lambda &= \frac{(x_4-x_2)(\imath y_4-\imath y_3) - (\imath y_4-\imath y_2)(x_4-x_3)}{(\imath y_4-\imath y_3)(x_1 - x_2)- (\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)(x_4-x_3)}\\ \end{alignat*} \end{minipage} }\\ We need to check that the denominator $(y_4-y_3)(x_1 - x_2)- (y_1 - y_2)(x_4-x_3)$ is not zero. Assume that its = then we would have $(y_4-y_3)(x_1 - x_2) = (y_1 - y_2)(x_4-x_3)$, which is equivalent to $\frac{y_4-y_3}{x_4-x_3} = \frac{y_1 - y_2}{x_1 - x_2}$. This would mean that the two lines are parallel and therefore $G_1 = G_2$ or $G_1 \cap G_2 = \varnothing$.\\ Thus we can assume that the denominator is not zero and therefore we can write $\lambda$ as a fraction of two elements in $L$. Let $L$ be a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$, with $L = conj(L)$. For $i = 1,2,3$ let $z_i = x_i + \imath y_i \in L$ with $z_1 \ne z_2$, and let $r > 0$ in $\mathbb{R}$ with $r^2 \in L$. Define \begin{equation*}\begin{aligned} G := \{\lambda z_1 + (1-\lambda)z_2 \mid \lambda \in \mathbb{R}\},\\ C := \{z = x + \imath y \in \mathbb{C} \mid \|z - z_3\| = r\}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} Assume $G \cap C \ne \emptyset$; then the following are equivalent: \begin{itemize} \item $z\in G \cap C$. \item There is a $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\lambda^2 a+ \lambda b + c = 0$ where \begin{align*} a &:= (x_1 - x_2)^2 + (\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)^2,\\ b &:= 2(x_1 - x_2)(x_2 - x_3) - 2(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)(\imath y_2 - \imath y_3),\\ c &:= (x_2 - x_3)^2 + (\imath y_2 - \imath y_3)^2 - r^2, \end{align*} and $z = \lambda z_1 + (1-\lambda)z_2$. \end{itemize} In this case $z \in L(\sqrt{w})$ for an $w \in L$.
nodes.label: lem:ConjClosed.Intersection_line_circle

nodes.statement: First we have to show $z \in G \cap C$ iff and only iff there exists a $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\lambda^2 a+ \lambda b + c = 0$ and $z = \lambda z_1 + (1-\lambda)z_2$. "$\Rightarrow:$" If z belongs to the intersection of G and C, then z satisfies the equations of C and G. Consequently \begin{align*} &&\|z - z_3\| &= r &&\mid 0\le \|\cdot\|\text{ and }0\le r\\ &\Leftrightarrow& \|z - z_3\|^2 &= r^2\\ &\Leftrightarrow& (x - x_3)^2 + (\imath y - \imath y_3)^2 &= r^2 &&\mid x = \lambda x_1 - \lambda x_2 + x_2 \text{ and }\\ &&&&&\mid y = \lambda y_1 - \lambda y_2 + y_2\\ &\Leftrightarrow& (\lambda x_1 - \lambda x_2 + x_2 - x_3)^2 + \\ &&(\imath (\lambda y_1 - \lambda y_2 + y_2 - y_3))^2 &= r^2\\ &\Leftrightarrow& \lambda ^2 ((x_1 - x_2)^2 + (\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)^2) + \\ &&\lambda (2(x_1 - x_2)(x_2 - x_3) - 2(\imath y_1 - \imath y_2)(\imath y_2 - \imath y_3)) + \\ &&(x_2 - x_3)^2 + (\imath y_2 - \imath y_3)^2 &= r^2\\ \end{align*} "$\Leftarrow:$" Since $z = \lambda z_1 + (1-\lambda)z_2$ we get $z$ in $G$ and can use the equations from the first part of the proof to show that $z$ is in $C$. Now we can show that there exists a $w \in L$ such that $z \in L(\sqrt{w})$.\\ Since we know that $z = \lambda z_1 + (1-\lambda)z_2$ and $z_1, z_2 \in L$ we only have to show that $\lambda \in L(\sqrt{w})$.
